units.summary: Shmuel instructs messengers to go to Rav (calling him Abba) and challenge his ruling on the transition of mentioning rain during the Festival.
During a famine in the days of Joel, the prophet convinces the people to sow their last bits of grain, resulting in a miraculous eleven-day growth cycle that saves the nation.

Rav Naḥman and Rabbi Yitzḥak share a meal where Rabbi Yitzḥak refuses to speak while eating for safety reasons, subsequently engaging in a series of teachings and a parting blessing once the meal concludes.

After being mocked for his ugliness by the emperor's daughter, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya tricks her into ruining her father's wine in expensive vessels to prove that wisdom, like wine, is best preserved in humble containers.
Rabbi Ami alludes to the famous legend of the marten and the pit, where a young man rescues a girl and they swear an oath of fidelity witnessed by the marten and the pit.
During a simultaneous famine and plague in the days of Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani, the Sages decided they could only pray for the relief of one affliction at a time and chose the plague.
When a decree forbade fasting in the days of Rabbi Zeira, he instructed the community to commit to the fast immediately so it would be credited to them, even if they could only perform it later.
Rabbi Yoḥanan encounters the young son of Reish Lakish and engages in a homiletical and legal discussion about tithing and testing God.
In a second encounter, Rabbi Yoḥanan is so impressed by the boy's wisdom that his intense gaze frightens the boy's mother, who pulls him away to avoid him suffering his father's fate.

After Rava's death, his elite students join Rav Pappa's academy but mock his teaching style by winking at one another when he offers explanations they find weak. Rav Pappa has a dream about the death of shepherds and, interpreting it as an omen regarding his students, bids them a final farewell the next day.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi overhears Rav Pappa praying to be saved from the embarrassment caused by Shimi's difficult questions, leading Shimi to stop challenging him.
Rav Daniel bar Ketina would inspect his garden and specify which beds needed water, and rain would fall only on those specific spots.
Ulla warns Babylonians to protect their vessels from imminent rain, but when no rain falls, he declares that Babylonian rain is as deceitful as the Babylonians themselves.
Ulla initially praises the cheapness of Babylonian dates as an aid to Torah study, but after they cause him physical distress at night, he changes his mind.
Shmuel defines the time to request rain based on when Tavut the bird hunter brings wood into his house.
Rav Pappa used to eat a loaf of bread for every parasang he traveled because he believed travel affected the bowels.
Mar Ukva visits Ginzak and is asked three questions he cannot answer, prompting him to travel to the study hall to find the solutions.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok recounts how his family once postponed the Ninth of Av fast due to Shabbat and then did not complete the fast because the following day was their ancestral festival.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yoḥanan would claim to be fasting until he reached his home as a pretext to leave the House of the Nasi.
When the Sages told the blind Rav Sheshet that other rabbis were wearing shoes on a fast day, he became angry and sarcastically suggested they might as well have eaten too.
Rav Yehoshua visited Rav Asi's home and was offered a choice meal while fasting, but he was told he could eat and make up the fast another day.
An incident is recounted where Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, bathed in cold water during the seven days of mourning for his sons.
An incident is recounted where Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, bathed in cold water throughout the mourning period for his sons.
Rav Yehuda appointed his son Rav Yitzḥak to expound publicly, and Rav Yitzḥak subsequently taught the laws of the Aneinu prayer.

During the time of Rabbi Yehuda Nesia, a calamity struck the community, leading to the decree of fasts. During a drought, Rabbi Yehuda Nesia wanted to extend the fast days beyond the standard thirteen, but Rabbi Ami stopped him to prevent over-burdening the community.
The people of Nineveh inquired of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi regarding the protocol for fasting for rain during the summer months in their specific climate.

An incident occurred involving Rabbi Halafta and Rabbi Hananya ben Teradyon where the prayer service on a fast day followed a unique Temple-style protocol. An incident occurred where a prayer leader in the presence of Rabbi Ḥalafta and Rabbi Ḥananya ben Teradyon followed a Temple-style liturgy, leading the Sages to clarify that such rituals are restricted to the Temple Mount.
The Gemara elaborates on the specific actions taken by the people of Nineveh to repent, including separating mother animals from their young and demolishing structures to return stolen materials.
When the Roman Empire decreed against Jewish practice, a matron advised the Jews to protest at night, leading them to cry out to Heaven for their rights as brothers.
The general Nicanor would daily wave his hand toward Jerusalem and threaten to conquer it.
Trajan executes the brothers Luleyanus and Pappas after a theological debate, only to be immediately executed himself by Roman officials.
Elders from Jerusalem traveled to their home cities to decree fasts following reports of blight in Ashkelon and wolf attacks on children.
Honi HaMe'aggel draws a circle and refuses to leave it until God sends rain, eventually resulting in such heavy rain that the people must retreat to the Temple Mount.
When rain fell before midday on a fast day in Lod, Rabbi Tarfon instructed the people to break their fast and celebrate, which they did.

Nakdimon ben Guryon borrows twelve wells of water from a Roman official for festival pilgrims, agreeing to pay a heavy fine if it does not rain by a certain date, and the deadline arrives during a drought. Nakdimon ben Guryon miraculously brings rain and then sunshine through prayer to fulfill a contract for water with a Roman officer.

Rabbi Elazar, feeling arrogant after much study, travels home and encounters an exceedingly ugly man. Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon insults a man's appearance and must follow him to his city to seek forgiveness, leading to a lesson on being 'soft like a reed.'
Rav and Shmuel, who avoided a dilapidated wall for thirteen years, finally walk past it when the meritorious Rav Adda bar Ahava is with them.
Rav Huna uses Rav Adda bar Ahava's merit to keep a dilapidated house from falling while he moves his wine, and the house collapses immediately after they exit.

Ilfa and Rabbi Yoḥanan leave their studies due to poverty, but Rabbi Yoḥanan returns after overhearing angels, eventually becoming the head of the academy while Ilfa remains a businessman who must prove his scholarship.
Naḥum of Gam Zu explains to his students that his severe physical disabilities were self-inflicted as a penance for failing to feed a poor man quickly enough before he died of hunger.

Naḥum of Gam Zu is sent to the Emperor with a gift of jewels that are stolen and replaced with earth, but through divine intervention, the earth becomes a miraculous weapon, leading to Naḥum's reward and the thieves' downfall.
Rav Naḥman bar Rav Ḥisda decrees a fast for a plague, leading to a legal debate and a scholarly exchange with Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak about leadership and honor.
When a plague skips Rav's neighborhood, a dream reveals it is due to the merit of a man who lends tools for burials rather than Rav's own merit.
A fire in Drokart avoids Rav Huna's neighborhood, and a dream reveals this was due to the merit of a woman who shared her oven.
Passage B introduces a new protagonist (Rav Yehuda) and a distinct event (a locust plague) that is independent of the fire in Drokart described in Passage A.

Abaye, curious about the superior heavenly merit of Abba the Bloodletter, sends two sages to test him by staying at his home and 'stealing' his rugs. The Sages test Abba the Bloodletter's piety by stealing his rugs and asking him to appraise them, only to find he held no suspicion and had already mentally renounced ownership for charity.
Rava is distressed that he receives fewer heavenly greetings than Abaye, but is comforted by the fact that his merit protects his city.

Rabbi Beroka Hoza'a encounters Elijah the Prophet in a market and is shown that a prison guard and two jesters are destined for the World-to-Come due to their secret acts of kindness and communal service.
As King Josiah lies dying, the prophet Jeremiah bends over him to ensure he is not complaining against God, only to hear him justifying the divine judgment.
Ulla reports an incident where wolves swallowed two children and excreted them, leading to a rabbinic inquiry.
Rabba bar bar Hana describes the immense height of Keren Ophel by noting that an Arab on a camel seen from the top looked like a tiny worm.
In the days of Shimon ben Shetaḥ, rain fell at ideal times resulting in unnaturally large produce that was preserved as a historical example.
During the construction of the Temple in Herod's time, rain fell only at night and cleared by morning so that the workers were never delayed.
Ḥoni HaMe’aggel draws a circle and refuses to move until God sends rain, successfully negotiating the intensity of the rainfall through successive prayers until the drought is broken.
Ḥoni HaMe’aggel falls into a miraculous seventy-year sleep and wakes to find that while his questions about the carob tree are answered, he is no longer recognized by his family or peers.

When a drought occurred, the Sages went to find Abba Ḥilkiyya, the grandson of Ḥoni, and found him working in his field. Abba Hilkiyya and his wife pray for rain on their roof, and he subsequently explains his eccentric but righteous behaviors to the visiting Sages.
Hanan HaNehba would be approached by children during droughts to pray for rain because of his humility.

Passage B introduces a new set of actors (Rabbi Zerika, Rav Safra, Rav Huna, and Rav Hisda) and a distinct practice regarding prayer for rain, serving as a comparative counter-example to the preceding story.
Passage B is a complete narrative about Rabbi Yona's humble method of praying for rain, distinct from the narrative in Passage A regarding his son Rabbi Mani's persecution by the house of the Nasi.
Rabbi Mani prays at his father's grave for relief from his persecutors, resulting in their horses being miraculously stuck until they agree to leave him alone.
Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elyashiv performs a series of miracles for Rabbi Mani regarding his in-laws and his wife's appearance, eventually reversing the beauty miracle when it causes domestic strife.
Two students ask Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elyashiv to pray for their wisdom, but he tells them he no longer has that power.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin leaves the academy of Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat to study with Rav Ashi.
The son of Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat miraculously provides figs for his father's hungry laborers, leading to a harsh rebuke from his father for bothering Heaven.
Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat sees a man gazing at his beautiful daughter and prays for her death so that she will not lead others to sin.
The donkey of Rabbi Yosei from Yokrat was so scrupulous that it would not return home if its hirers accidentally left extra items or money on its back.
Elazar of Birta gives his daughter's dowry to charity collectors for orphans, leading to a miracle where his granary is found overflowing with wheat.
Rabbi Yehuda Nesia decrees a fast for rain that fails, leading him to lament his generation's spiritual standing compared to the prophet Samuel.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish are informed of a fast too late to accept it properly, but decide to observe it regardless.
Oshaya the Youngest is tormented by the Nasi's servants for a critical parable he told during a drought, but he is saved by the testimony of his townsmen.
When Rabbi's fast fails to bring rain, Ilfa leads the prayer and the wind and rain respond immediately to his words.
Rav encounters a prayer leader whose prayer brings rain because of his selfless devotion to teaching the children of the poor.
Rav Nahman's self-deprecating anguish over his failed prayer for rain causes Heaven to respond with rain.
Rabba discusses why his generation's prayers are not answered compared to Rav Yehuda's generation, despite their superior Torah study.
Rav Yehuda causes a famine after seeing bread wasted, but later brings rain by removing his shoe after witnessing the desperation of the people.
Rav Mari witnesses angels turning sand into flour during the famine but warns the people it is a miracle that will not last.
Rava decrees a fast in Hagrunya and rain falls after Rabbi Elazar of Hagrunya shares a propitious dream.
After Rava accidentally kills a man during a flogging, King Shapur's mother protects him from the King's wrath by demonstrating Rava's power to bring rain on command.
Rav Pappa eats porridge during a drought-induced fast, leading to a sarcastic remark from Rav Naḥman bar Ushpazti.
Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa commands the rain to stop while he is traveling for his own comfort and to start again once he is safely home.
Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's wife feigns baking to hide her poverty, but a miracle occurs when a suspicious neighbor investigates, filling her oven with real bread.
Rabbi Ḥanina's wife convinces him to pray for wealth, but after receiving a golden table leg from heaven, they choose to return it to ensure their reward in the afterlife remains whole.
When Rabbi Ḥanina's daughter accidentally lights the Shabbat lamp with vinegar, he declares that God can make vinegar burn as well as oil, and it does.
To prove his goats were not damaging neighbors' property, Rabbi Ḥanina decrees they should bring back bears on their horns, which they do.
A woman whose house beams are too short seeks help from Rabbi Ḥanina, who prays for them to lengthen, resulting in a permanent architectural miracle.
Rabbi Ḥanina meticulously preserves chickens left at his door, eventually trading them for goats, all of which he gives to the original owner when he returns years later.

The impoverished Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat faints and dreams of a conversation with God, where he declines to have the world destroyed and rebuilt for his sake, receiving a promise of great reward in the afterlife instead.
Rabbi Ḥama bar Ḥanina successfully brings rain after a failed fast by rebuking the sky for its impudence.
Levi successfully prays for rain but is punished with lameness for the disrespectful tone he used toward God.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Lulyani overhears clouds planning to rain on Ammon and Moab and successfully prays for the rain to be redirected to Israel.
Rabbi Eliezer decrees thirteen fasts that fail to bring rain, and as the congregation leaves the synagogue, he rebukes them by asking if they have prepared their graves.
After Rabbi Eliezer's prayers fail to bring rain, Rabbi Akiva leads the prayer and rain falls immediately.
Rabba describes a vision of the angel Ridya, who looks like a calf and commands the celestial and subterranean waters to provide rain.
When rain falls early during a fast decreed by Shmuel HaKatan, he tells a parable to explain that God granted the rain quickly only to stop hearing their voices.
On another occasion, rain falls after sunset following a fast, and Shmuel HaKatan again rebukes the people's assumption that this indicates their merit.

In Lod, after a fast was decreed and rain fell, the people ate and drank before reciting Hallel. Rav Pappa arrived at a synagogue, decreed a fast, and when rain fell before noon, he instructed the people to recite Hallel.
The Mishna lists historical calamities that occurred on the seventeenth of Tammuz and the Ninth of Av.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel describes the custom of the daughters of Jerusalem dancing in the vineyards on the 15th of Av and Yom Kippur to find spouses.
The returning exiles use a lottery system to expand four priestly watches into twenty-four, with the prophets ensuring the new order remains permanent.
Abraham expresses concern to God about Israel's survival after the Temple's destruction, leading God to establish the reading of the sacrificial order as a means of atonement.
When the exiles returned to Jerusalem and found no wood for the altar, certain families donated their own, leading the prophets to establish their permanent right to do so.

Passage B introduces a new set of actors (the descendants of those who deceived the authorities) and begins a distinct narrative about their specific heroic actions during the period of the royal decrees, separate from the general wood-offering history in Passage A.
To bypass a Greek decree forbidding offerings, pious Jews disguised their first fruits as building materials and successfully tricked the road guards.
The descendants of Salmai of Netophat bypassed Greek blockades by fashioning their wood offerings into ladders and tricking guards into believing they were for a dovecote.
Rav arrives in Babylonia and initially intends to stop the community from reciting Hallel on the New Moon until he notices they are skipping sections, leading him to conclude it is a valid custom.
A Roman officer saves Rabban Gamliel from an execution decree by committing suicide after securing a promise of a place in the World-to-Come.
During the First Temple's destruction, young priests throw the Temple keys toward heaven and leap into the flames.
